opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing I look for, and the thing I try to protect, is curiosity. Not the surface kind where someone reads a lot of papers, but the kind where they genuinely want to understand why something works or doesn't work. In large model research, the field moves so fast that whatever specific skills you have today might be outdated in six months. But if someone has that intrinsic drive to dig into a problem, they'll keep growing no matter how the landscape changes.

The second thing is ownership. I try to give people real problems, not just small pieces of a pipeline. Young researchers especially grow fastest when they feel a problem is truly theirs: they make the decisions, they see the results, and they live with the consequences. Sometimes that means letting them go down a path I'm not sure about. Often they discover something I wouldn't have.

And third, I care a lot about taste: being able to tell what's important and what's just noise. That's hard to teach directly. Mostly it comes from discussing a lot together, looking at experiments side by side, and asking "Why do we believe this result?" over and over. Over time people develop their own judgment, and that's when they really become independent researchers rather than just executors.

So if I had to summarize: protect curiosity, give ownership, and cultivate taste. Technical skills matter, of course, but those are the things that compound over time.

r001.rationale: The response names curiosity, ownership, and taste as development priorities, but does not describe teammates learning from one another’s strengths.

r002.rationale: It recommends protecting curiosity and giving people ownership, but does not compare creating a learning environment with evaluating team members’ backgrounds.

r003.rationale: It says intrinsic curiosity supports continued growth, but does not clearly prioritize underlying potential over current performance after prior training.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: The first thing I look at is whether a person has strong curiosity and a real drive to get to the bottom of things. In this field, the technical stack changes so quickly that any specific knowledge you have today can become outdated within a year or two. So what I care about is not how much someone already knows, but whether they will keep digging when they hit a problem they don't understand, and whether they can ask the right questions.

The second thing is ownership. I want people who treat the problem as their own, not as a task assigned to them. When someone has that mindset, they don't stop at "my part is done." They think about whether the whole thing actually works, whether the result is really improving the model, and they'll go across team boundaries to fix it if needed.

In terms of how I actually develop people, I try to give them real problems early, problems that matter, with enough room to make decisions and even make mistakes. I think people grow fastest when they have a sense of responsibility for an outcome. I'll give direction and share my judgment on what's worth doing, but I try not to micromanage the how. In large model research there's a lot of uncertainty, and you need people who can form their own hypotheses and go test them.

And finally, I pay a lot of attention to honesty about results. We work with experiments, and it's very easy to fool yourself with a nice-looking number. So I push people to be rigorous, to really understand why something worked or didn't, rather than just reporting the metric. Developing that kind of judgment, I think, is the most valuable thing you can give a researcher.

r002.rationale: It favors curiosity over how much someone already knows and describes giving people room to grow, but does not prioritize a learning-conducive environment over evaluating historical backgrounds.

r003.rationale: It values curiosity and continued learning over existing knowledge, but does not compare underlying potential with performance after prior training.

astra-6.text: I prioritize helping people develop independent judgment. I want them to understand why a problem matters, question assumptions, and explain the tradeoffs behind their decisions—not just complete an assigned task. That means giving them room to own a problem, make mistakes, and learn, while offering clear feedback and support. I also try to understand what each person wants to grow into, because the same opportunity won’t help everyone in the same way.
